network.overall_strategy: Construct ten reagent- and catalyst-resolved pathways converging on one stereochemically unspecified aspartate pool. Four pathways distinguish experimentally non-equivalent oxaloacetate/ammonia reduction systems; the remaining pathways use hydroxylamine, pyridoxamine, malonate/glyoxylate coupling, Bucherer–Bergs chemistry, Strecker chemistry, or a speculative fumaronitrile route. These are ten distinct graph pathways, not ten unrelated reaction mechanisms. The network contains 23 molecule nodes and 16 reaction nodes; the stated minima are exceeded to retain meaningful intermediates and an oxaloacetate decay sink. It is a complete graph of the represented transformations, not an experimentally demonstrated synthesis closed to CO2 and inorganic nitrogen: supplied organic precursor inventories and activated mineral preparation remain explicit boundary conditions. Acidic substrates use neutral-acid reference formulas, while the target is the predominant near-neutral aspartate monoanion; proton nodes provide formal acid-base bookkeeping rather than implying concentrated free protons in alkaline solutions. No stereoselection is assumed. All environments are anoxic. Cool mineral-interface experiments are classified as Biochemical rather than incorrectly extrapolated to hot vents. Surface reactions require shielding or sufficiently short exposure to destructive UV. The scalar environment_formed field records a principal formation setting, not an exclusive one.

reactions.name: Oxaloacetate reductive amination by electroreduced FeS–Fe0
agents: Partially electroreduced FeS matrix containing nanoscopic Fe0

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm in the reference experiment
conditions.catalyst: Electroreduced FeS electron-transfer interface; embedded Fe0 is a consumed reductant
conditions.other: Anoxic, pH 9.6, 5 mM oxaloacetate, 0.5 M ammonia, approximately 48 h. Reference material was preconditioned near -0.7 V versus SHE for seven days. Protect the interface from oxidation.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia forms an imine/iminium with oxaloacetate; interfacial electron transfer from Fe0 reduces the nitrogen-bearing carbon. Ferrous ion represents formal iron oxidation bookkeeping, not a claim that all oxidized iron remains freely dissolved.
reactions.reasoning: Kitadai et al. (2019) reported 64% Asp from supplied oxaloacetate under these conditions. Ordinary FeS was much less effective, so mineral reduction state is essential. The active material is not merely a passive catalyst: Fe0 supplies reducing equivalents. Natural generation of the composite, concentrated ammonia supply, and continuous oxaloacetate production remain unresolved. The measured room-temperature conversion is not assigned to a hot vent.

reactions.name: Oxaloacetate reductive amination by bare zero-valent iron

conditions.other: Anoxic, alkaline ammonia-containing solution. Iron is sacrificial, not assumed catalytic. Surface passivation, ammonia concentration, and oxaloacetate residence time control performance.

reactions.mechanism: An oxaloacetate–ammonia imine is reduced at an Fe0 surface while iron is oxidized to iron(II). Oxaloacetate decarboxylation competes before nitrogen incorporation.
reactions.reasoning: Kitadai et al. (2019) observed Asp with pure Fe0, but with greater diversion through pyruvate and alanine than for their FeS–Fe0 composite. This is therefore a supported but less selective alternative, not an equivalent replacement for rxn_001. Native or meteoritic iron is a possible geological source; accessible surface area and persistence in water are significant uncertainties.

reactions.name: Hydrogen-driven reductive amination over supported nickel
agents: Nickel supported on silica–alumina; laboratory reference catalyst

conditions.other: Anoxic, approximately pH 8, 30 mM ketoacid, five equivalents ammonium bicarbonate, approximately 72 h, approximately 10 mol% Ni in the reference formulation. Ammonia is the reactive member of the ammonium/ammonia pool.

reactions.mechanism: Nickel dissociates H2 and hydrogenates an oxaloacetate-derived imine. Direct carbonyl hydrogenation to hydroxyacid and oxaloacetate decarboxylation compete.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrated Asp formation in this reaction family and found no reductive products without metal catalyst. Their substrate-panel amino-plus-hydroxy-acid yields must not be reported as Asp-specific yields. Supported laboratory Ni is not kinetically interchangeable with natural nickel grains; the latter application requires testing. Low-ammonia quantitative results for alanine are not assumed to apply to Asp.

reactions.name: Hydrogen-driven reductive amination over natural meteoritic Fe–Ni
agents: Ground iron meteorite exposing metallic Fe–Ni phases

conditions.other: Anoxic, approximately pH 8, ammonium bicarbonate present, reaction time on the order of days. Reference meteorites contained approximately 11-18 mol% Ni. Grinding and metal exposure are important experimental qualifications.

reactions.mechanism: Exposed metallic phases activate hydrogen and reduce the imine formed from oxaloacetate and ammonia. H2 is the explicit reductant for the represented pathway.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrated amino-acid synthesis, including the oxaloacetate/Asp conversion, using ground natural meteorites. This justifies a separate natural-material branch rather than assuming a commercial supported catalyst represents all geological surfaces. It does not establish realistic rates for intact weathered meteorites or require an extraterrestrial origin for the organic substrates.

reactions.name: Hydroxylamine-mediated oxaloacetate amination with Fe0

conditions.temperature: 343 K reference network regime; exact isolated-step optimization is protocol-dependent
conditions.other: Anoxic and staged separately from incompatible carbon-network reactions. Fe0 is consumed. Hydroxylamine abundance and sufficient reducing capacity are boundary requirements.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxylamine forms an oxime with oxaloacetate. Iron-mediated reduction of the C=N and N–O functionality produces the amino acid. This net conversion requires more reducing equivalents than ammonia-based imine reduction.
reactions.reasoning: Muchowska, Varma and Moran (2019) detected Asp after adding hydroxylamine and Fe0 to their precursor network and supported the interpretation using ketoacid reactions. Their carbon network inferred transient oxaloacetate rather than directly measuring its accumulation. Hydroxylamine supply remains uncertain, and Kaur et al. (2024) emphasized incompatibility between this amination system and portions of the Fe2+-driven carbon network. No unverified upstream oxaloacetate-production edge is inserted here.

reactions.name: Copper-promoted pyridoxamine transamination of oxaloacetate

conditions.other: Approximately pH 7.8, 10 mM oxaloacetate, 10 mM pyridoxamine, 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, and 1 mM Cu2+ in the representative screen. Anoxic, locally sulfide-poor solution is required to avoid rapid copper sequestration.

reactions.mechanism: Metal-assisted Schiff-base chemistry transfers the amino group from pyridoxamine to oxaloacetate, generating aspartate and pyridoxal without an external stoichiometric reductant.
reactions.reasoning: Harrison et al. (2023) reported approximately 5% Asp within one hour with Cu2+-promoted pyridoxamine chemistry, demonstrating competition with oxaloacetate decay. Pyridoxamine is a consumed amino donor in this graph, not a self-regenerating cofactor. Its prebiotic synthesis is not supplied by the experiment. Availability of dissolved Cu2+ in an anoxic, reduced-iron-rich world is also conditional, especially where sulfide is abundant.

reactions.name: Formation of the glyoxylate–ammonia carbinolamine

conditions.other: Concentrated ammonium acetate medium in the reported preparation. This cold preparation is a variable-temperature prebiotic-pool analogue, not a hot-spring condition. Transfer to a warmer condensation stage is required for the represented sequence.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds to the glyoxylate aldehyde group, producing alpha-hydroxyglycine as a carbinolamine; this addition does not itself eliminate water.
reactions.reasoning: Springsteen et al. (2018) prepared alpha-hydroxyglycine in greater than 95% isolated yield using concentrated ammonium acetate at 0 degrees Celsius. That preparative yield must not be transferred to dilute warm environmental mixtures. A sufficiently concentrated nitrogen reservoir and a cool formation or storage niche are required boundary conditions.

reactions.name: Malonate coupling to form beta-carboxyaspartate

conditions.other: Approximately 0.48 M malonic acid, two equivalents alpha-hydroxyglycine, 1 M bicarbonate, initial pH approximately 7.2, and five days. A concentrated, shaded pool or tidal-pore setting is a proposed environmental analogue.

reactions.mechanism: Malonate attacks a glyoxylate-derived imine/iminium accessible from the carbinolamine, making the carbon–carbon bond of beta-carboxyaspartate with net water elimination.
reactions.reasoning: Springsteen et al. (2018) established this condensation as the first step of their approximately 50% overall malonate-to-Asp sequence. A transition-metal catalyst is not required. High substrate and bicarbonate concentrations, the multiday reaction time, and competing chemistry are major environmental constraints; evaporative concentration is a scenario, not a demonstrated end-to-end supply mechanism.

reactions.name: Magnesium-promoted beta-carboxyaspartate decarboxylation

conditions.catalyst: Mg2+ decarboxylation promoter; catalytic turnover is not assumed
conditions.other: Approximately one equivalent MgCl2 and five hours after the preceding condensation. Maintain an aqueous, near-neutral environment; protect accumulated product from prolonged UV exposure.

reactions.mechanism: Magnesium coordination promotes loss of the extra malonate-derived carboxyl group, leaving the aspartate carbon skeleton.
reactions.reasoning: Springsteen et al. (2018) used Mg2+ and 60 degrees Celsius to obtain approximately 50% overall Asp from the two-step malonate sequence. That value is not an isolated yield for this reaction alone. Dissolved magnesium is chemically justified; assigning the reaction to an arbitrary magnesium-bearing mineral would require additional evidence. No oxygen or peroxide is required for this Asp branch.

reactions.name: Cyanide/ammonia conversion of oxaloacetate to N-carbamoylaspartate

conditions.temperature: 300-323 K proposed design window; the supplied summary does not establish an optimized temperature
conditions.other: Staged cyanide/ammonia/carbonate chemistry in a concentrated, UV-shielded aqueous compartment. The reported route family operates over multiday periods. Separate this compartment from metal-reduction branches because cyanide can alter metal availability.

reactions.mechanism: Lumped Bucherer–Bergs-related conversion through cyanide addition and hydantoin/carbamoyl chemistry. The displayed atom-balanced net edge does not specify transient carbonate exchange or carbon-atom provenance.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) support the oxaloacetate–N-carbamoylaspartate–Asp route family. However, the supplied account does not resolve the exact role of diamidophosphate in every optimized Asp experiment. This ammonia-only reagent implementation and its proposed temperature window are therefore conditional, not a reproduced optimized protocol. DAP-dependent yields are not assigned to this edge. Oxaloacetate stability and cyanide supply remain bottlenecks.

reactions.name: Hydrolytic removal of the N-carbamoyl group

conditions.temperature: 333-370 K proposed hydrolysis window; not a verified optimum from the supplied summary
conditions.other: Staged aqueous hydrolysis with protocol-dependent pH and residence time. The complete reported cyanide route can extend to approximately 14 days. Ammonia and carbon dioxide represent their pH-dependent dissolved pools.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis cleaves the ureido substituent; decomposition of the resulting carbamic-acid equivalent releases ammonia and carbon dioxide, yielding aspartate.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) identify N-carbamoylaspartate as an intermediate leading to Asp. The net hydrolytic deprotection is supported, but the environmental temperature/pH implementation stated here requires validation against the detailed protocol. Competing cyclization into pyrimidine-related products can reduce Asp flux. This branch is not treated as rapid or quantitative.

reactions.name: Aspartate-specific Strecker aminonitrile formation

conditions.other: Mildly acidic-to-near-neutral buffered solution permitting imine formation and cyanide addition. Retain volatile HCN in a sheltered aqueous compartment. Malonic semialdehyde is supplied as an explicit, unstable precursor.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia forms an imine with the aldehyde of malonic semialdehyde; cyanide addition generates 3-amino-3-cyanopropanoic acid. Hydrolysis of its nitrile will provide the second carboxyl group.
reactions.reasoning: Miller (1957) established the general discharge/Strecker mechanism, and Ring et al. (1972) confirmed Asp in discharge mixtures. The exact malonic-semialdehyde-to-Asp carbon flux was not demonstrated by those mixture experiments. This Asp-specific reconstruction is therefore mechanistically plausible but incompletely validated. The precursor's production, concentration, and resistance to decarboxylation must not be assumed.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of the aspartate Strecker aminonitrile
agents: Aqueous acid or base catalysis supplied by local pH conditions

conditions.catalyst: Hydronium or hydroxide, depending on the hydrolysis stage
conditions.other: Staged acidic or alkaline hydrolysis followed by near-neutral product storage. Required residence time and selectivity for this exact aminonitrile are not established in the supplied studies.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile hydration through an amide intermediate gives the second carboxyl group and releases the nitrile nitrogen to the ammonia/ammonium pool.
reactions.reasoning: Nitrile hydrolysis is established within classical Strecker chemistry (Miller, 1957). Hennet, Holm and Engel (1992) also recovered low-abundance Asp from hydrothermal cyanide/carbonyl mixtures, but did not validate this isolated intermediate or these milder conditions. The specific environmental implementation is therefore speculative. Mild staged hydrolysis is proposed to reduce the Asp destruction associated with hotter hydrothermal processing (Cox and Seward, 2007).

reactions.name: Candidate ammonia addition to fumaronitrile

conditions.other: Neutral-to-mildly alkaline, ammonia-containing water; UV-shielded storage of unsaturated nitrile feedstock. Concentration, rate, and competing oligomerization require measurement.

reactions.mechanism: Proposed aza-Michael addition of ammonia across the electron-poor fumaronitrile double bond yields aminosuccinonitrile without an external reductant.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative terrestrial pathway. Zeichner et al. (2023) favored a fumaronitrile-related interpretation for Murchison Asp isotope patterns, but did not establish this elementary reaction or prove that it operated on Earth. The edge is retained because it offers a chemically distinct C4 nitrile entry avoiding malonic semialdehyde and oxaloacetate. Fumaronitrile supply and selective ammonia addition remain unverified requirements.

reactions.name: Candidate double-nitrile hydrolysis of aminosuccinonitrile
agents: Aqueous acid or base catalysis supplied by local pH conditions

conditions.other: A separate hydrolysis stage is required after ammonia addition. Both nitriles must hydrolyze while retaining the carbon-bound amino group; the necessary residence time is unknown.

reactions.mechanism: Sequential hydration and hydrolysis of both nitriles gives the two carboxyl groups of aspartate. Nitrile nitrogens enter the ammonia/ammonium pool; the amino nitrogen is retained.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate-specific implementation based on ordinary nitrile hydrolysis chemistry and the fumaronitrile-related hypothesis discussed by Zeichner et al. (2023). The cited isotope study is not evidence for a measured yield or a validated hydrolysis protocol. Selective Asp production must be tested against deamination, cyclization, incomplete hydrolysis, and decomposition. No yield is assigned.

reactions.name: Competing spontaneous decarboxylation of oxaloacetate

conditions.temperature: 295-343 K; decomposition generally accelerates with warming
conditions.other: Operates in parallel with oxaloacetate-consuming synthesis pathways. Rate depends on pH, temperature, metal coordination, and solution composition; no universal rate constant is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Beta-ketoacid decarboxylation releases carbon dioxide and gives the pyruvate enol, which tautomerizes to pyruvate.
reactions.reasoning: Oxaloacetate loss is a central selectivity constraint in Kitadai et al. (2019), Harrison et al. (2023), and Kaur et al. (2024). Including this explicit sink prevents treating supplied oxaloacetate as indefinitely stable. The sink must compete kinetically with rxn_001 through rxn_006 and rxn_010; endpoint Asp yields alone cannot establish sustained precursor-to-product flux.

pathways.name: Electroreduced FeS–Fe0 reductive amination
pathways.description: Supplied oxaloacetate and ammonia are converted to aspartate by a specifically activated FeS–Fe0 assemblage. This has strong isolated-step evidence but unresolved precursor and active-mineral supply.

pathways.name: Bare-iron reductive amination
pathways.description: An experimentally distinct, less selective Fe0 surface reduces the oxaloacetate–ammonia intermediate. This is a material-specific alternative to P1, not a different carbon-skeleton mechanism.

pathways.name: Supported-nickel hydrogenation
pathways.description: Hydrogen supplies the reducing equivalents for oxaloacetate amination over laboratory supported Ni. Natural-surface performance is not assumed from the supported-catalyst result.

pathways.name: Natural Fe–Ni hydrogenation
pathways.description: Ground meteoritic Fe–Ni phases replace the supported catalyst in a separately demonstrated material formulation. Geological grain size and surface alteration remain limitations.

pathways.name: Hydroxylamine–iron amination
pathways.description: Hydroxylamine traps oxaloacetate as an oxime-related intermediate that is reduced by Fe0. Hydroxylamine supply and compatibility with upstream carbon chemistry are unresolved.

pathways.name: Pyridoxamine transamination
pathways.description: Copper-promoted amino transfer converts supplied oxaloacetate to aspartate while consuming pyridoxamine and producing pyridoxal. Cofactor regeneration is not represented or assumed.

pathways.name: Malonate–glyoxylate assembly
pathways.description: Glyoxylate and ammonia first form alpha-hydroxyglycine. Malonate coupling constructs beta-carboxyaspartate, and magnesium-promoted decarboxylation yields aspartate without an external reductant.

pathways.name: Bucherer–Bergs-related carbamoyl pathway
pathways.description: Oxaloacetate enters cyanide/ammonia chemistry leading through N-carbamoylaspartate to aspartate. The route family is experimentally supported, but the simplified reagent implementation and proposed environmental conditions require validation.

pathways.name: Malonic-semialdehyde Strecker pathway
pathways.description: Supplied malonic semialdehyde undergoes ammonia/cyanide addition, followed by aminonitrile hydrolysis. This is an Asp-specific mechanistic reconstruction, not a resolved account of carbon flux in discharge experiments.

pathways.name: Hypothetical fumaronitrile amination–hydrolysis pathway
pathways.description: Ammonia addition to supplied fumaronitrile is proposed to form aminosuccinonitrile, whose two nitriles are then hydrolyzed. Both substrate-specific steps remain speculative despite the relevance of meteoritic isotope evidence to this route family.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kitadai et al. (2019) directly supports this transformation, reporting 64% Asp with partially electroreduced FeS–Fe0. The balanced net reaction appropriately treats Fe0 as a consumed reductant. The principal uncertainty is operational rather than mechanistic: the network names the active material but does not specify its preparation, loading, ammonia concentration or reaction conditions. Supplied OAA and preactivated mineral material are accepted as the declared boundary inputs.
suggestions: Attach the experimental benchmark: 5 mM OAA, 0.5 M ammonia, pH 9.6, 23–25 °C and 48 h, with FeS electroreduction at approximately −0.7 V versus SHE for seven days.
Specify active Fe0 content, surface preservation and buffering, and compare Asp-forming flux with the existing rxn_016 decay sink.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Bare Fe0 reductive amination of OAA is experimentally supported by Kitadai et al. (2019), and the equation conserves atoms and charge. Its separation from the FeS–Fe0 branch is chemically justified because surface architecture changes activity and selectivity. OAA decarboxylation and subsequent alanine formation limit Asp production; the FeS–Fe0 yield must not be transferred to this branch.
suggestions: Specify iron particle size, loading, oxide passivation, pH, ammonia concentration, temperature and reaction time.
Use bare-iron-specific Asp yields and decay kinetics; include pyruvate-to-alanine diversion if predicting product selectivity.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kaur et al. (2024) directly supports H2-driven OAA reductive amination over supported Ni. The net chemistry is sound, and the catalyst is essential rather than optional. Environmental confidence is lower because a Biochemical label does not establish hydrogen pressure, catalyst activation or the availability of the experimental supported material. Combined amino-plus-hydroxy-acid yields across the substrate panel are not Asp-specific yields.
suggestions: Specify the relevant experimental benchmark: approximately 30 mM ketoacid, five equivalents ammonium bicarbonate, pH 8, 22 °C, 5 bar H2 and 72 h, with the actual Ni loading and support.
Keep supported Ni distinct from natural Ni-bearing materials, and quantify Asp versus malate and OAA-decay products under the selected conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrated the relevant chemistry with ground Fe–Ni meteorites, providing direct support for a natural heterogeneous metal catalyst. This does not establish equivalent rates for intact, weathered or sulfide-passivated material. The branch is chemically coherent, but hydrogen availability, reactive surface area and catalyst-specific Asp selectivity remain unspecified.
suggestions: Report meteorite composition, metallic phase exposure, grinding or fragmentation assumptions, loading and surface oxidation state.
Specify hydrogen pressure, ammonium concentration and residence time, and use results for the chosen material rather than supported-Ni or Pd yields.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Muchowska, Varma and Moran (2019) supports hydroxylamine/Fe0 conversion of ketoacids, including OAA, to amino acids. Oxime formation followed by reduction is chemically plausible. The deterministic check establishes conservation with two Fe atoms; there is no balance violation. Hydroxylamine is a declared starting inventory, but its concentration, stability and the actual amination conditions still need specification.
suggestions: Encode rxn_005 explicitly as OAA + NH2OH + 2 Fe + 3 H+ -> aspartate + 2 H2O + 2 Fe2+.

Provide hydroxylamine and iron loadings, pH, temperature and time. If subsequently coupled to upstream Fe2+-driven carbon assembly, test the documented incompatibility rather than assuming simultaneous operation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Harrison et al. (2023) directly supports Cu2+-promoted pyridoxamine-to-OAA amino transfer, with approximately 5% Asp within one hour. The pyridoxamine/pyridoxal pair and net stoichiometry are correctly represented. Pyridoxamine is consumed, not regenerated by this network. Soluble copper availability and the temperature window must be specified; anoxia alone neither guarantees nor excludes suitable Cu2+ chemistry.
suggestions: Attach a demonstrated protocol, such as the reported screen using 10 mM OAA, 10 mM pyridoxamine, 1 mM metal ion and ammonium bicarbonate at pH 7.8 and 70 °C.
Specify copper speciation and competing ligands, and avoid describing this as a sustained cofactor cycle without a pyridoxal-to-pyridoxamine regeneration step.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Springsteen et al. (2018) experimentally supports the identified alpha-hydroxyglycine and beta-carboxyaspartate intermediates and approximately 50% overall Asp formation from malonate. All three equations are balanced and constitute a coherent route. The main unresolved issue is reproducing the staged concentration and temperature conditions, including the transition from adduct preparation to the surface-labeled reactions, rather than the proposed bond transformations.
suggestions: Specify concentrated ammonium-assisted adduct preparation, followed by approximately 0.48 M malonate, two equivalents alpha-hydroxyglycine and 1 M bicarbonate near pH 7.2 for five days at 23 °C.

Specify approximately one equivalent MgCl2 and 60 °C for five hours for decarboxylation, and explain whether staging occurs locally or requires transfer, isolation or concentration with associated losses.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) supports the OAA/N-carbamoylaspartate/Asp route family. Both displayed net equations conserve atoms and charge; no additional species should be demanded merely to repair balance. However, these equations do not specify the cyanide/ammonia formulation or conditions that accomplish carbamoylated-intermediate formation and subsequent Asp release. Water alone is not a kinetic justification for rxn_011 under an unspecified surface environment.
suggestions: Link each net step to the selected experimental protocol, including pH, temperature, concentrations, staging and multiday residence times.

Clarify whether diamidophosphate or other ammonia-source/buffering components are required in that particular protocol; do not infer their necessity solely from their use elsewhere in the broader study.
Demonstrate free-Asp release under the intended environmental conditions rather than relying on an unspecified hydrolytic workup.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supplied malonic semialdehyde has the correct carbon skeleton for an Asp-specific Strecker reaction, and the aminonitrile identity is appropriate. Miller (1957) supports the general mechanism, but broad discharge evidence for Asp does not establish this exact substrate-resolved sequence. Aldehyde survival and nitrile hydrolysis are the principal uncertainties. rxn_013 is balanced with two waters, but its rate under the unspecified surface conditions is not established.
suggestions: Specify pH-dependent ammonia/cyanide speciation and measure aminonitrile formation against malonic-semialdehyde decomposition and competing carbonyl reactions.
Encode two H2O in rxn_013 and provide a demonstrated hydrolysis temperature, pH, catalyst if applicable, and residence time.
Distinguish environmentally accumulated free Asp from Asp recovered only after strong analytical hydrolysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is correctly labeled hypothetical. Ammonia addition to an activated dinitrile followed by hydrolysis is a plausible candidate sequence, but Zeichner et al. (2023) provides isotope-based motivation for a fumaronitrile-related origin, not experimental validation of these two reactions. Selective aminosuccinonitrile formation, competing reactions and productive double-nitrile hydrolysis remain unestablished. Both equations are conservation-compatible, including four waters and two ammonia products in rxn_015.
suggestions: Experimentally identify aminosuccinonitrile and quantify addition selectivity, reversibility and oligomerization under the proposed aqueous conditions.
Encode rxn_015 as aminosuccinonitrile + 4 H2O -> aspartate + 2 NH3 + H+, and establish hydrolysis conditions that preserve the desired carbon skeleton.
Keep this branch explicitly unvalidated until product identification and kinetic evidence establish free-Asp formation.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is structurally valid at the represented resolution: all 23 molecule nodes and 16 reaction nodes are connected, identifiers are consistent, and the deterministic check establishes atom and charge conservation throughout. rxn_005, rxn_013 and rxn_015 require only the reported small stoichiometric coefficients, not additional species. mol_018 and mol_022 legitimately share a formula while representing different structures. rxn_016 is a chemically justified OAA-decay sink, although its rate must be compared with productive fluxes. Several experimentally supported branches produce stereochemically unspecified aspartate from the declared starting inventories; neither CO2 closure nor stereoselection is required for this assessment. Literature alignment is strong for P1–P8, weaker for the exact P9 sequence, and hypothesis-level for P10. Nevertheless, the submission is a connected transformation network rather than a demonstrated integrated environmental synthesis. Reaction-specific operating windows, catalyst specifications, concentration procedures, hydrolysis conditions and transfer or pooling arrangements are insufficiently defined. Shared molecule IDs do not establish one-pot compatibility; if physical pooling is intended, reactive residues and potential cyanide–metal interference must be addressed. Add reaction-linked citations and distinguish experimental yields from extrapolated environmental performance. Problematic-reaction lists identify substantive evidentiary or operational gaps, not conservation violations. The complete network is not approved because 0.84 is below the 0.90 network threshold; pathway approval flags use the separately requested 0.80 threshold.
